message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease, move‑in inspection report, and any receipts for repairs you paid.
• Request a written receipt for the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Texas Property Code §92.001 requires landlords to keep premises in a habitable condition (plumbing, heating, electrical, structural safety).
• Landlord must repair any major defects that affect health or safety. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If repairs are not made within a reasonable time, you may withhold rent or make the repairs yourself and deduct the cost (but only if you follow the proper procedure). | | **Rent Payment & Late Fees** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for inspections, repairs, or showing the unit to prospective tenants or buyers. | • Keep a log of all entries. | | **Privacy** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (except emergencies).
• You have the right to quiet enjoyment of the premises. | • If you feel your privacy is being violated, document the incidents and consider contacting the Texas Attorney General’s office. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the Texas Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing laws, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Attorney General or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party may terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a written notice of termination at least 30 days before the lease ends. | • Keep a copy of any notice you receive. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit, 30‑day notice to vacate for non‑payment, 60‑day notice for lease termination).
• Eviction must go through the court; landlords cannot forcibly remove you. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you receive an eviction notice, you have 30 days to file a response in court. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper procedure (written notice, reasonable time to repair, etc.). | • Keep receipts and document the defect. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas has no statewide rent‑control laws. | • Be aware that rent increases are generally limited only by what the lease allows. | | **Utilities** | • The lease specifies who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease and keep records of payments. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • The lease may restrict subletting; if it does, you must get written permission. | • If you need to sublet, ask the landlord in writing and keep a copy of the agreement. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords are not required to provide renter’s insurance, but it’s highly recommended. | • Consider obtaining renter’s insurance to cover personal property and liability. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, rent amount, due date, late fees, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, move‑in inspection, correspondence with the landlord, and any repair receipts. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – Landlords must give you written notice for entry, rent increases, or lease termination. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Write a formal notice of any maintenance issue and keep a copy. 5. **Keep Records of Payments** – Save receipts or bank statements for rent and utilities. 6. **Know Your Eviction Rights** – If you receive an eviction notice, file a response in court within the deadline. ### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | |----------|----------------| | **Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection Division** | File complaints, find legal aid. | | **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** | Fair housing complaints, resources. | | **Texas Tenants’ Rights Organization** | Local advocacy groups, legal clinics. | | **Legal Aid of North Texas** | Free or low‑cost legal assistance. | | **Texas Property Code** | Full statutory text (available online). | --- **Disclaimer:** This information is intended for general informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. If you have a specific legal issue, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
